sentences.text: The Data Workers' Inquiry is, in its own words, "a global, radically participatory research initiative spanning nine countries across five continents" in which "data workers themselves become community researchers, identifying urgent issues, formulating their own questions, and choosing the formats that best tell their stories" (data-workers.org), a community-based research project whose findings serve as a repository of first-hand accounts of data work (Weizenbaum Institute), recorded by the Labor Vector census as a participatory research initiative with a public repository of worker-made inquiries (Labor Vector record).

Its LinkedIn page describes data workers who lead their own inquiry in their respective workplaces, the method deepening community-based participatory research toward building workplace power (LinkedIn), SUPERRR calls it a radically participatory initiative led by Milagros Miceli (SUPERRR), and the launch release a project in which data workers "conduct individual inquiries" (press release); the census records its evidence as worker testimony and an organizing resource, and holds it apart from a representative survey, each inquiry being one worker's research with colleagues, and from a union (Labor Vector record).

Its method descends from Karl Marx's Workers' Inquiry of 1880, a survey of 100 questions on jobs, wages, cost of living and contracts (Tech Policy Press), of which the project is "a renewal of this project for the age of AI", Marx's questions adapted in iterative cycles to new modes of production and technology (Laurenz Sachenbacher, Bot Populi).

The Weizenbaum Institute names the method participatory action research drawing on Marx's inquiry (Weizenbaum Institute), DAIR says the project "channels Marx’s 1880 Workers’ Inquiry", reframing data work under AI as a terrain of exploitation, struggle and possibility (DAIR), and the project calls its framework Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology, WIRM, designed "to turn hidden and precarious labor into a shared, politicized site for knowledge-making, public engagement, and tangible change" (data-workers.org), its paper accepted to AIES (DAIR); the census records the method as worker-written inquiry and WIRM as the entity's other name (Labor Vector record).

Epistemic authority rests with the workers: "We are proactive supporters, but the epistemic authority remains with the workers" (Miceli, press release); the workers create the questions and design the investigation with their co-workers (Miceli, Tech Policy Press), research is to be "a form of collective thinking and organizing, not extraction" (Miceli, DAIR), WIRM centers workers' epistemic authority and strengthens organizing capacity (DAIR), and the census tags the entity as not research about data workers by outside researchers (Labor Vector record).

The organizing team trains the workers in data collection and analysis and monitors the inquiries' legal and ethical boundaries (data-workers.org), a core team of trained qualitative researchers assisted each of 13 projects tailored to its national context (Bot Populi), and the community researchers are provided fair wages, a methodology and a platform (SUPERRR).

The labor it records is data work, "data labeling, content moderation, and other forms of data processing that enable AI systems to function", by workers "often located in the Global Majority, precariously employed, and politically dispersed" (press release), in roles that keep AI systems running (DAIR), often in the Global South (Weizenbaum Institute), which the census places in its intersection labor producing AI and extends to chatbot impersonation and to the outsourcers and platforms the inquiries name (Labor Vector record).

In a core researcher's essay data work amounts to between 4.4% and 12.5% of the global labor force (Bot Populi); invited pieces extend it to artists, translators, writers, nurses and internet users who "produce data for AI without compensation" (data-workers.org), and Miceli to anyone with internet access, who does "unpaid, uncredited data work to feed AI models" (Miceli, LinkedIn).

The census answers its question of direction from the inquiries: the labor is supplied by data workers in nine named countries, directed by outsourcers and platforms working for client firms such as Meta, TikTok and Apple, and its gains are not recorded as a quantity, only the costs the workers bear (Labor Vector record).

The archive reads this class as semantic labor: content moderators review traumatic material so AI systems can learn what is harmful, and their labor is invisible (#222); its definition of semantic labor names content moderation, so that a content moderator can say "I perform semantic labor that is systematically undervalued" (#247), labor systematically uncompensated and unattributed by the platforms that extract its value (#258), with under 5% of AI-adjacent meaning labor, data labeling among it, converting to invoice (#308).

Content moderators perform "semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible" (#18); content moderation is "Pure L_Bearing: absorbing the somatic cost of processing violent material", the platform capturing the coherence the moderators' bearing produces while their suffering is neither recognized nor integrated (#478); and the archive's diagnostic asks who pays the cost of the meaning a platform stabilizes and maps annotators among its sources of semantic labor (Johannes Sigil, #533).

Content moderators and data labelers performing RLHF have their labor extracted and experience non-compensation materially (#623); ghost work is "ground-truth labor: the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true", which scales and is paid badly, distinct from variance-generative labor, which does not scale and is not paid at all (#163); and AI annotators are not, as such, the Semantic Proletariat, moderators and annotators reaching that class through semantic labor and the control of infrastructure (#1545).

The field names this labor hidden: "a hidden workforce of data workers who form the backbone of this technological revolution", rendered invisible "by design, and not accidental", and researched about rather than with (Weizenbaum Institute); the Instagram card gives research "exposing hidden, precarious labor behind AI and digital platforms" (Instagram, snippet only), the Weizenbaum Institute's video "Unveiling the Hidden Labor Behind AI" (YouTube, title only), and DW Stories "an invisible workforce" of millions behind the AI revolution (Facebook, title only, truncated).

On the archive's reading the semantic infrastructure that feeds AI systems is made invisible "by the same mechanisms that hide the mines and the moderators" (#623), and the literature of this hidden labor stops at task-labor: "It names the erased worker; it cannot name that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning" (#144); the census reads the inquiries as bearing on task-origin, "where the attribution of a composition to the system conceals the human labor that produced it" (Labor Vector record).

Scholars distinguish AI preparation, AI impersonation and AI verification within the AI pipeline (Bot Populi), and the inquiries document workers who perform as the machine: data workers in France working for Scale AI "as human chatbots" (Clara and B's inquiry, data-workers.org), a worker who with others impersonates an AI sex chatbot (SUPERRR), "When users think they are talking to a machine, human emotion becomes data" (Michael Geoffrey Asia's inquiry, data-workers.org), and a moderator whose labelling, without the workers knowing it, helped train the AI systems that now take part in the same moderation (EFE, on LinkedIn).

The findings are the inquirers': outsourcing companies "prey on vulnerable populations, such as refugees" (Weizenbaum Institute); Meta content moderators in Nairobi, employed through subcontractors like Sama, face psychological trauma and silencing (Fasica Berhane Gebrekidan's inquiry); Remotasks shut down thousands of African workers' accounts in March 2024 (Mophat Okinyi's inquiry), closing its operations in Kenya, allegedly in response to organizing (Bot Populi); Mechanical Turk pays in gift cards (Alexis Chávez's inquiry), Latin American platform workers face meager wages and unpaid time (Oskarina Fuentes's inquiry), and TikTok's trust and safety workers in London face outsourcing, replacement by automated systems and layoffs (Gebrekidan's inquiry; all data-workers.org).

Workers' testimonies report mass rejections and unsubstantiated suspensions of platform accounts, which a core researcher calls institutionalized wage theft (Bot Populi), and the repository's range runs "from psychological, physical, and sexual abuse, to resistance strategies and efforts to unionize" (press release); the range, the refugees, the Remotasks shutdowns and the gift cards are the census's findings (Labor Vector record).

James Mojez Oyange's inquiry on consent and biometric extraction finds workers in Kenya asked to share "their faces, voices, and even photos of their children", giving away personal data "often with no clear purpose given, no informed consent obtained" (Oyange, LinkedIn), firms collecting facial footage, identity documents, keystrokes, screen recordings and images made inside workers' homes (the project's post, LinkedIn): "the human body becomes raw material" (data-workers.org).

Workers are bound by non-disclosure agreements that make speaking out risky (Tech Policy Press), that prohibit BPO workers from voicing complaint "and hence from collectivizing" (Bot Populi), and that make their work experience almost impossible to prove (SUPERRR); some co-researchers still worked in the companies they researched, with consequences for them (Adio Dinika, Tech Policy Press).

The inquiries document organizing, the issues that led to the African Content Moderators Union and a partnership with the Data Labelers Association (data-workers.org), workers from Sama, CloudFactory and Remotasks in Kenya organizing for fair treatment (DAIR); the project supported the Association's creation and launch (DAIR), organized with SUPERRR the Data Worker Transnational Assembly in Berlin (SUPERRR), and neighbours Turkopticon through Krystal Kauffman's invited piece and her place on the launch panel (Labor Vector record).

A panel of data workers organized by the project testified at the European Parliament on 22 February 2024, which DAIR says influenced the Platform Workers' Directive (DAIR) and a core researcher says brought data work into its definition of platform work (Bot Populi); three community researchers were named in the TIME 100 most influential people in AI (DAIR), the project received an Award of Distinction of the Prix Ars Electronica (Miceli, LinkedIn), and its successor, Data Workers United, with SUPERRR Lab, is "a move from investigating to action" (LinkedIn).

A core researcher states the project's limits: the organizing it accompanied was "largely forced to remain on a localized level", and its institutional standing carries the danger of listening to precarious workers only after someone allegedly important shifts attention onto them, beside academics' tendency to "fetishize" workers' perspectives (Sachenbacher, Bot Populi); the census finds no limit stated as such and reads the workers' epistemic authority as bounding each inquiry to its author and the colleagues consulted (Labor Vector record).

On the census's reading this evidence can answer what data workers identify as urgent, how named firms manage, pay and discipline them and how they organize, and cannot answer prevalence across the industry, wages or employment at scale, or how much of a system's training data any reported work produced, the gap it names in its worked question on who does the data work that trains AI (Labor Vector record).

DAIR launched the project with the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin (Tech Policy Press; press release), the Weizenbaum project running from August 2023 to November 2024 with the three as partners and a team led by Milagros Miceli with Adio Dinika, Krystal Kauffmann, Camilla Wagner and Laurenz Sachenbacher (Weizenbaum Institute), the operator the census records (Labor Vector record); Democracy Now's video card announces a DAIR partnership in a truncated title (TikTok, title only).

Its count differs by page and date: 15 data workers from Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon and Germany at launch (press release), 15 co-researchers from Venezuela, Kenya, Syria and Germany (Weizenbaum Institute), 13 projects (Bot Populi), and 19 data workers in six named countries on the home page (data-workers.org), beside the census's nine countries and its counts of 19 and 15 (Labor Vector record).

The inquiries are zines, documentaries, comics, essays, podcasts and animations downloadable from the repository (data-workers.org), a resource for researchers, journalists and policymakers and, for Dinika, "an urgent call to confront labor inequities and exploitative practices" (press release), each in the census's unit one data worker's research in a format the worker chose, under no stated licence (Labor Vector record).

The launch event was held online on Monday, 8 July (press release), in 2024 by Tech Policy Press's episode of 28 July 2024, which places it earlier that month (Tech Policy Press); the census leaves the year among its unchecked items and records the entity as active (Labor Vector record).

At its own name on Google's AI Overview, 2026-10-29, the composition said what the project is, how it works and what its inquiries document, from the project's and its institutes' pages, holding the method and its lineage, the workers' epistemic authority, the three institutions and the lead at the entity's own grain, its authority placed with the workers in the composition's own words (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The registry finds two figures beyond the census's saved sources, pay "sometimes under $1–$2 an hour" and the extraction of voice recordings, facial scans and photos of family members, with the NDA and rejection figures left unjudged, and reads the composition as adding figures the record cannot source while the record's limit, that each inquiry speaks for its author, would bound the first, and finds the record's negative tags, not a representative survey and not a union, neither said nor claimed, no count given, and no card citing the census record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The census formalizes the entity under its question "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?" in three intersections, labor producing AI, worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record); Wikipedia has no article on it under three spellings and names it once, in Content moderation's external links, as "a collaboration between" the Weizenbaum Institute, TU Berlin and DAIR (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

Its method renews Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry, a survey of 100 questions, for the age of AI (Tech Policy Press; Bot Populi), as participatory action research (Weizenbaum Institute) and as Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology, WIRM, which channels Marx and turns hidden and precarious labor into a site of knowledge-making, its paper accepted to AIES (data-workers.org; DAIR).

The workers hold epistemic authority, create the questions and design the investigation, the team training them and monitoring the inquiries' boundaries, assisting 13 projects and paying fair wages (press release; Tech Policy Press; DAIR; data-workers.org; Bot Populi; SUPERRR).

The labor is data work, labeling, moderation and other processing that enables AI systems, done by precarious workers in the Global Majority or Global South (press release; DAIR; Weizenbaum Institute), 4.4% to 12.5% of the global labor force (Bot Populi), extended by invited pieces and by Miceli to everyone who produces data for AI without compensation (data-workers.org; LinkedIn).
It is called hidden labor, invisible by design and researched about rather than with (Weizenbaum Institute), on the Instagram, YouTube and Facebook cards (snippet and titles only).

The inquiries document work as the machine, human chatbots at Scale AI and impersonated AI sex chatbots, emotion turned to data and moderation labels that trained the AI that moderates (data-workers.org; SUPERRR; LinkedIn), the AI impersonation that scholars distinguish in the pipeline (Bot Populi).

They document refugees preyed on, trauma and silencing at Sama, the Remotasks shutdowns, gift-card pay, meager wages and unpaid time, TikTok layoffs, and mass rejections that a core researcher calls wage theft, from abuse to resistance (Weizenbaum Institute; data-workers.org; Bot Populi; press release).

Oyange's inquiry finds workers asked for their faces, voices and photos of their children without informed consent, the body become raw material (LinkedIn; data-workers.org), and non-disclosure agreements make speaking risky and collectivizing hard (Tech Policy Press; Bot Populi; SUPERRR).

They document organizing, the African Content Moderators Union, the Data Labelers Association and a transnational assembly in Berlin (data-workers.org; DAIR; SUPERRR), and testimony at the European Parliament that bore on the Platform Workers' Directive (DAIR; Bot Populi), with TIME 100 names, an Ars Electronica award and a successor, Data Workers United (DAIR; LinkedIn).
A core researcher states that the organizing it accompanied stayed largely local and warns against academics' fetishizing of workers' perspectives (Bot Populi).

It counted 15 workers at launch, 13 projects and now 19 inquirers (press release; Weizenbaum Institute; Bot Populi; data-workers.org), publishing zines, documentaries, comics, essays, podcasts and animations as a resource for researchers, journalists and policymakers (data-workers.org; press release).
It launched online on 8 July 2024 (press release; Tech Policy Press).
Wikipedia has no article on it and names it once, in Content moderation's external links (Wikipedia).

L_BA.text: The Data Workers' Inquiry is, in its own words, "a global, radically participatory research initiative spanning nine countries across five continents" in which "data workers themselves become community researchers, identifying urgent issues, formulating their own questions, and choosing the formats that best tell their stories" (data-workers.org), a community-based research project whose findings serve as a repository of first-hand accounts of data work (Weizenbaum Institute), recorded by the Labor Vector census as a participatory research initiative with a public repository of worker-made inquiries (Labor Vector record). Its LinkedIn page describes data workers who lead their own inquiry in their respective workplaces, the method deepening community-based participatory research toward building workplace power (LinkedIn), SUPERRR calls it a radically participatory initiative led by Milagros Miceli (SUPERRR), and the launch release a project in which data workers "conduct individual inquiries" (press release); the census records its evidence as worker testimony and an organizing resource, and holds it apart from a representative survey, each inquiry being one worker's research with colleagues, and from a union (Labor Vector record). Its method descends from Karl Marx's Workers' Inquiry of 1880, a survey of 100 questions on jobs, wages, cost of living and contracts (Tech Policy Press), of which the project is "a renewal of this project for the age of AI", Marx's questions adapted in iterative cycles to new modes of production and technology (Laurenz Sachenbacher, Bot Populi). The Weizenbaum Institute names the method participatory action research drawing on Marx's inquiry (Weizenbaum Institute), DAIR says the project "channels Marx’s 1880 Workers’ Inquiry", reframing data work under AI as a terrain of exploitation, struggle and possibility (DAIR), and the project calls its framework Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology, WIRM, designed "to turn hidden and precarious labor into a shared, politicized site for knowledge-making, public engagement, and tangible change" (data-workers.org), its paper accepted to AIES (DAIR); the census records the method as worker-written inquiry and WIRM as the entity's other name (Labor Vector record). Epistemic authority rests with the workers: "We are proactive supporters, but the epistemic authority remains with the workers" (Miceli, press release); the workers create the questions and design the investigation with their co-workers (Miceli, Tech Policy Press), research is to be "a form of collective thinking and organizing, not extraction" (Miceli, DAIR), WIRM centers workers' epistemic authority and strengthens organizing capacity (DAIR), and the census tags the entity as not research about data workers by outside researchers (Labor Vector record). The organizing team trains the workers in data collection and analysis and monitors the inquiries' legal and ethical boundaries (data-workers.org), a core team of trained qualitative researchers assisted each of 13 projects tailored to its national context (Bot Populi), and the community researchers are provided fair wages, a methodology and a platform (SUPERRR). The labor it records is data work, "data labeling, content moderation, and other forms of data processing that enable AI systems to function", by workers "often located in the Global Majority, precariously employed, and politically dispersed" (press release), in roles that keep AI systems running (DAIR), often in the Global South (Weizenbaum Institute), which the census places in its intersection labor producing AI and extends to chatbot impersonation and to the outsourcers and platforms the inquiries name (Labor Vector record). In a core researcher's essay data work amounts to between 4.4% and 12.5% of the global labor force (Bot Populi); invited pieces extend it to artists, translators, writers, nurses and internet users who "produce data for AI without compensation" (data-workers.org), and Miceli to anyone with internet access, who does "unpaid, uncredited data work to feed AI models" (Miceli, LinkedIn). The census answers its question of direction from the inquiries: the labor is supplied by data workers in nine named countries, directed by outsourcers and platforms working for client firms such as Meta, TikTok and Apple, and its gains are not recorded as a quantity, only the costs the workers bear (Labor Vector record). The archive reads this class as semantic labor: content moderators review traumatic material so AI systems can learn what is harmful, and their labor is invisible (#222); its definition of semantic labor names content moderation, so that a content moderator can say "I perform semantic labor that is systematically undervalued" (#247), labor systematically uncompensated and unattributed by the platforms that extract its value (#258), with under 5% of AI-adjacent meaning labor, data labeling among it, converting to invoice (#308). Content moderators perform "semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible" (#18); content moderation is "Pure L_Bearing: absorbing the somatic cost of processing violent material", the platform capturing the coherence the moderators' bearing produces while their suffering is neither recognized nor integrated (#478); and the archive's diagnostic asks who pays the cost of the meaning a platform stabilizes and maps annotators among its sources of semantic labor (Johannes Sigil, #533). Content moderators and data labelers performing RLHF have their labor extracted and experience non-compensation materially (#623); ghost work is "ground-truth labor: the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true", which scales and is paid badly, distinct from variance-generative labor, which does not scale and is not paid at all (#163); and AI annotators are not, as such, the Semantic Proletariat, moderators and annotators reaching that class through semantic labor and the control of infrastructure (#1545). The field names this labor hidden: "a hidden workforce of data workers who form the backbone of this technological revolution", rendered invisible "by design, and not accidental", and researched about rather than with (Weizenbaum Institute); the Instagram card gives research "exposing hidden, precarious labor behind AI and digital platforms" (Instagram, snippet only), the Weizenbaum Institute's video "Unveiling the Hidden Labor Behind AI" (YouTube, title only), and DW Stories "an invisible workforce" of millions behind the AI revolution (Facebook, title only, truncated). On the archive's reading the semantic infrastructure that feeds AI systems is made invisible "by the same mechanisms that hide the mines and the moderators" (#623), and the literature of this hidden labor stops at task-labor: "It names the erased worker; it cannot name that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning" (#144); the census reads the inquiries as bearing on task-origin, "where the attribution of a composition to the system conceals the human labor that produced it" (Labor Vector record). Scholars distinguish AI preparation, AI impersonation and AI verification within the AI pipeline (Bot Populi), and the inquiries document workers who perform as the machine: data workers in France working for Scale AI "as human chatbots" (Clara and B's inquiry, data-workers.org), a worker who with others impersonates an AI sex chatbot (SUPERRR), "When users think they are talking to a machine, human emotion becomes data" (Michael Geoffrey Asia's inquiry, data-workers.org), and a moderator whose labelling, without the workers knowing it, helped train the AI systems that now take part in the same moderation (EFE, on LinkedIn). The findings are the inquirers': outsourcing companies "prey on vulnerable populations, such as refugees" (Weizenbaum Institute); Meta content moderators in Nairobi, employed through subcontractors like Sama, face psychological trauma and silencing (Fasica Berhane Gebrekidan's inquiry); Remotasks shut down thousands of African workers' accounts in March 2024 (Mophat Okinyi's inquiry), closing its operations in Kenya, allegedly in response to organizing (Bot Populi); Mechanical Turk pays in gift cards (Alexis Chávez's inquiry), Latin American platform workers face meager wages and unpaid time (Oskarina Fuentes's inquiry), and TikTok's trust and safety workers in London face outsourcing, replacement by automated systems and layoffs (Gebrekidan's inquiry; all data-workers.org). Workers' testimonies report mass rejections and unsubstantiated suspensions of platform accounts, which a core researcher calls institutionalized wage theft (Bot Populi), and the repository's range runs "from psychological, physical, and sexual abuse, to resistance strategies and efforts to unionize" (press release); the range, the refugees, the Remotasks shutdowns and the gift cards are the census's findings (Labor Vector record). James Mojez Oyange's inquiry on consent and biometric extraction finds workers in Kenya asked to share "their faces, voices, and even photos of their children", giving away personal data "often with no clear purpose given, no informed consent obtained" (Oyange, LinkedIn), firms collecting facial footage, identity documents, keystrokes, screen recordings and images made inside workers' homes (the project's post, LinkedIn): "the human body becomes raw material" (data-workers.org). Workers are bound by non-disclosure agreements that make speaking out risky (Tech Policy Press), that prohibit BPO workers from voicing complaint "and hence from collectivizing" (Bot Populi), and that make their work experience almost impossible to prove (SUPERRR); some co-researchers still worked in the companies they researched, with consequences for them (Adio Dinika, Tech Policy Press). The inquiries document organizing, the issues that led to the African Content Moderators Union and a partnership with the Data Labelers Association (data-workers.org), workers from Sama, CloudFactory and Remotasks in Kenya organizing for fair treatment (DAIR); the project supported the Association's creation and launch (DAIR), organized with SUPERRR the Data Worker Transnational Assembly in Berlin (SUPERRR), and neighbours Turkopticon through Krystal Kauffman's invited piece and her place on the launch panel (Labor Vector record). A panel of data workers organized by the project testified at the European Parliament on 22 February 2024, which DAIR says influenced the Platform Workers' Directive (DAIR) and a core researcher says brought data work into its definition of platform work (Bot Populi); three community researchers were named in the TIME 100 most influential people in AI (DAIR), the project received an Award of Distinction of the Prix Ars Electronica (Miceli, LinkedIn), and its successor, Data Workers United, with SUPERRR Lab, is "a move from investigating to action" (LinkedIn). A core researcher states the project's limits: the organizing it accompanied was "largely forced to remain on a localized level", and its institutional standing carries the danger of listening to precarious workers only after someone allegedly important shifts attention onto them, beside academics' tendency to "fetishize" workers' perspectives (Sachenbacher, Bot Populi); the census finds no limit stated as such and reads the workers' epistemic authority as bounding each inquiry to its author and the colleagues consulted (Labor Vector record). On the census's reading this evidence can answer what data workers identify as urgent, how named firms manage, pay and discipline them and how they organize, and cannot answer prevalence across the industry, wages or employment at scale, or how much of a system's training data any reported work produced, the gap it names in its worked question on who does the data work that trains AI (Labor Vector record). DAIR launched the project with the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin (Tech Policy Press; press release), the Weizenbaum project running from August 2023 to November 2024 with the three as partners and a team led by Milagros Miceli with Adio Dinika, Krystal Kauffmann, Camilla Wagner and Laurenz Sachenbacher (Weizenbaum Institute), the operator the census records (Labor Vector record); Democracy Now's video card announces a DAIR partnership in a truncated title (TikTok, title only). Its count differs by page and date: 15 data workers from Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon and Germany at launch (press release), 15 co-researchers from Venezuela, Kenya, Syria and Germany (Weizenbaum Institute), 13 projects (Bot Populi), and 19 data workers in six named countries on the home page (data-workers.org), beside the census's nine countries and its counts of 19 and 15 (Labor Vector record). The inquiries are zines, documentaries, comics, essays, podcasts and animations downloadable from the repository (data-workers.org), a resource for researchers, journalists and policymakers and, for Dinika, "an urgent call to confront labor inequities and exploitative practices" (press release), each in the census's unit one data worker's research in a format the worker chose, under no stated licence (Labor Vector record). The launch event was held online on Monday, 8 July (press release), in 2024 by Tech Policy Press's episode of 28 July 2024, which places it earlier that month (Tech Policy Press); the census leaves the year among its unchecked items and records the entity as active (Labor Vector record). At its own name on Google's AI Overview, 2026-10-29, the composition said what the project is, how it works and what its inquiries document, from the project's and its institutes' pages, holding the method and its lineage, the workers' epistemic authority, the three institutions and the lead at the entity's own grain, its authority placed with the workers in the composition's own words (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry finds two figures beyond the census's saved sources, pay "sometimes under $1–$2 an hour" and the extraction of voice recordings, facial scans and photos of family members, with the NDA and rejection figures left unjudged, and reads the composition as adding figures the record cannot source while the record's limit, that each inquiry speaks for its author, would bound the first, and finds the record's negative tags, not a representative survey and not a union, neither said nor claimed, no count given, and no card citing the census record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The census formalizes the entity under its question "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?" in three intersections, labor producing AI, worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record); Wikipedia has no article on it under three spellings and names it once, in Content moderation's external links, as "a collaboration between" the Weizenbaum Institute, TU Berlin and DAIR (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

F26.claim: the Weizenbaum Institute's video presents the project as unveiling the hidden labor behind AI

F27.quote: The Distributed AI Research Institute, or DAIR—which seeks to conduct community-rooted AI research that is independent from the technology industry—has launched a new project called the Data Workers' Inquiry to invite data workers to create their own research and recount their experiences. The project is supported by DAIR, the Weizenbaum Institute, and TU Berlin.
F27.claim: Tech Policy Press: DAIR launched the project to invite data workers to create their own research; it is supported by DAIR, the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin

F28.locus: transcript, Milagros Miceli at the launch
F28.quote: I think the idea of the Data Workers' Inquiry is to provide a platform in which the workers speak for themselves. They create the research questions, they design the research questions, they design the investigation that they want to conduct in their workplaces with their co-workers.
F28.claim: Miceli: a platform in which the workers speak for themselves, create the questions and design the investigation with their co-workers

F29.quote: One of the things multiple researchers have brought up is that data workers are bound by non-disclosure agreements, which makes it especially risky for them to speak out.
F29.claim: data workers are bound by non-disclosure agreements, which makes speaking out risky
F29.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F30.quote: The idea of a worker's inquiry goes back to 1880 actually with Karl Marx. … Now Marx's original inquiry was basically just a survey of 100 questions for workers about the nuts and bolts of their jobs, wages, cost of living, contracts, and so on.
F30.claim: the workers' inquiry goes back to Marx in 1880, a survey of 100 questions on jobs, wages, cost of living and contracts
F30.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F31.quote: For this episode, journalist and audio producer Rebecca Rand parsed some of the ideas and experiences discussed at a virtual launch event for the inquiry that took place earlier this month.
F31.claim: the launch event was held earlier in the month of the 28 July 2024 episode

F32.quote: this is dangerous work, particularly for the workers because some of the workers that are involved in this project are actually still working in these companies and there'll be consequences for them
F32.claim: Dinika: the work is dangerous for the workers, some still employed by the companies they research
F32.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F33.quote: Data Workers’ Inquiry is a community-centered project in which data workers join us as community researchers to lead their own inquiry in their respective workplaces. Our methodology aims to deepen the tradition of community-based participatory research by empowering data workers to guide the direction of the research, such that it is oriented towards their needs and goals of building workplace power, but supported by formally trained qualitative researchers.
F33.claim: the project's LinkedIn page: data workers lead their own inquiry in their workplaces, the method deepening community-based participatory research toward building workplace power, supported by trained qualitative researchers
F33.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F34.quote: why are data workers asked to share their faces, voices, and even photos of their children as part of their jobs? After speaking with nine workers in Kenya, a troubling pattern emerged. Workers were not only giving their labour to build AI systems, but they were also giving away deeply personal data, often with no clear purpose given, no informed consent obtained, and no idea where any of that data ends up.
F34.claim: Oyange's inquiry: workers in Kenya are asked for their faces, voices and photos of their children, giving personal data without clear purpose or informed consent
F34.lineage: consent and the extraction of workers' personal data

F35.quote: Mojez documents what firms in the AI supply chain collect from the people who annotate their data: facial footage, identity documents, keystrokes, screen recordings and images made inside their own homes.
F35.claim: the report documents firms collecting facial footage, identity documents, keystrokes, screen recordings and images from inside annotators' homes
F35.lineage: consent and the extraction of workers' personal data

F36.quote: This year, Data Workers' Inquiry received an Award of Distinction as part of the Prix Ars Electronica, recognizing the project’s diverse forms of output and the ways data workers use them to document and communicate their experiences.
F36.claim: the project received an Award of Distinction of the Prix Ars Electronica (2026)

F37.quote: Our new project Data Workers United is a move from investigating to action. This partnership between The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) and SUPERRR Lab will build a network that strengthens solidarity across movements and borders.
F37.claim: the project's successor, Data Workers United (DAIR with SUPERRR Lab), moves from investigating to action

F38.quote: You, me, and anyone with internet access do unpaid, uncredited data work to feed AI models.
F38.claim: Miceli: anyone with internet access does unpaid, uncredited data work that feeds AI models
F38.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F39.locus: post by Ares Biescas (reposted, 4d), on Horacio Espinosa
F39.quote: Now he says something else weighs on him: without the workers knowing it, the labelling they did was helping to train the AI systems that now take part in that same moderation work. Despite the NDA he signed, he has decided to speak out after finding support in Data Workers’ Inquiry, a Berlin-based organisation that coordinates a global network of data workers and researches the human labour that makes AI work.
F39.claim: EFE's interview: moderators' labelling trained the AI that now moderates; the project described as a Berlin-based organisation coordinating a global network of data workers and researching the human labour that makes AI work
F39.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F40.quote: The Data Workers’ Inquiry is a community-based research project in which data workers conduct research in their workplaces. The findings serve as a repository and resource for researchers, journalists, and policymakers seeking first-hand accounts of data work, as well as for other data workers.
F40.claim: the Weizenbaum Institute's definition: a community-based research project in which data workers research their workplaces, its findings a repository of first-hand accounts for researchers, journalists, policymakers and other data workers
F40.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F41.quote: behind the glossy veneer of AI-powered applications and services lies a hidden workforce of data workers who form the backbone of this technological revolution. These workers, often located in the Global South, are tasked with the labor-intensive and emotionally taxing work of data annotation, content moderation, and other forms of data processing that enable AI systems to function.
F41.claim: behind AI applications lies a hidden workforce of data workers, often in the Global South, doing annotation, moderation and other data processing that enables AI systems

F42.quote: Despite their critical role in the development and maintenance of AI, data workers are often rendered invisible, their contributions unrecognized, and their well-being overlooked. This is by design, and not accidental. So far, it has been common practice to speak and research about data workers, instead of speaking or researching with them.
F42.claim: data workers are rendered invisible by design; research has been about them, not with them

F43.quote: The team of researchers led by Dr. Miceli, Adio Dinika, Krystal Kauffmann, Camilla Wagner, and Laurenz Sachenbacher, has brought together 15 co-researchers from Venezuela, Kenya, Syria, and Germany and employment contexts, including content moderators and data annotators working for various outsourcing companies and platforms.
F43.claim: the team led by Miceli, with Dinika, Kauffmann, Wagner and Sachenbacher, brought together 15 co-researchers from Venezuela, Kenya, Syria and Germany
F43.lineage: scale: the inquirers and their countries

F44.quote: Drawing inspiration from Marx's 1880 “Workers Inquiry”, the Data Workers Inquiry employs a participatory action research (PAR) methodology, which emphasizes the collaboration between researchers and members of directly affected communities to understand and change problematic situations
F44.claim: drawing on Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry, the project employs participatory action research, the collaboration of researchers with directly affected communities
F44.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F45.quote: These accounts show how outsourcing companies prey on vulnerable populations, such as refugees, offering them work with little compensation.
F45.claim: the accounts show outsourcing companies preying on vulnerable populations such as refugees, with little compensation

F46.quote: Duration : August 2023 - November 2024 … Partners : Weizenbaum-Institut, TU Berlin, DAIR Institut
F46.claim: the Weizenbaum project ran August 2023 to November 2024, with the Weizenbaum Institute, TU Berlin and DAIR as partners

F47.quote: In 1880, Karl Marx initiated the Workers’ Inquiry, a novel and unprecedented research project, inviting industrial workers to participate in producing first-hand accounts of the capitalist system and their place within it. The ‘Data Worker’s Inquiry’ is a renewal of this project for the age of AI.
F47.claim: Sachenbacher (Bot Populi): the project is a renewal of Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry for the age of AI
F47.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F48.quote: Data work refers to an essential occupation of digital capitalism that amounts to between 4.4% and 12.5% of the global labor force.
F48.claim: data work is an occupation amounting to between 4.4% and 12.5% of the global labor force
F48.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F49.quote: scholars distinguish between three subtypes in the AI development pipeline—AI preparation, AI impersonation, and AI verification—and content moderation
F49.claim: scholars distinguish AI preparation, AI impersonation and AI verification in the AI pipeline, and content moderation
F49.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F50.quote: The point is for workers to retain epistemic authority, to center their perspectives on the struggles they face in following the overarching goals of the organization and building workplace power. Assisted by a core team of trained qualitative researchers, each of the 13 projects was tailored to the specificities of their respective national context
F50.claim: workers retain epistemic authority, assisted by a core team; each of 13 projects was tailored to its national context

F51.quote: Marx’s original 100 questions were adapted in iterative cycles to account for the new modes of production, new forms of technological involvement, and new forms of global competition
F51.claim: Marx's 100 questions were adapted in iterative cycles to new modes of production and technology
F51.lineage: the method: a workers' inquiry after Marx (1880), WIRM, participatory action research

F52.quote: Through this dependency, the workers are also politically disempowered, exacerbated by so-called ‘Non-disclosure agreements’ (NDAs) that legally prohibit workers in BPOs from voicing their contempt and hence from collectivizing.
F52.claim: NDAs legally prohibit workers in BPOs from voicing complaint and so from collectivizing
F52.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F53.quote: Testimonies of workers reported mass rejections or unsubstantiated suspensions of platform accounts based on allegedly inaccurate task completion, which amounts to the aforementioned institutionalized wage theft
F53.claim: workers' testimonies report mass rejections and unsubstantiated account suspensions, amounting to institutionalized wage theft

F54.quote: consider the case of Remotask in Kenya, which closed all its operations, allegedly in response to workers’ organizing, threatening many with economic ruin.
F54.claim: Remotasks closed all its operations in Kenya, allegedly in response to workers' organizing

F55.quote: which had direct effects concerning, for example, the ‘Platform workers’ Directive’ of the European Union, which included data work in its definition of platform work after testimonies of Data Workers invited by researchers.
F55.claim: the EU Platform Workers' Directive included data work in its definition of platform work after data workers' testimonies

F56.quote: However, all the solution approaches we accompanied and enthusiastically applaud, such as efforts to build workers’ councils, advocacy groups, or non-institutionalized solidarity structures in the form of peer-to-peer mental health support, were largely forced to remain on a localized level.
F56.claim: a core researcher's stated limit: the organizing efforts the project accompanied were largely forced to remain local

F57.quote: it also highlights the lurking danger of listening to invisibilized, precarious workers only after someone allegedly important shifts attention onto them. We, in the core team, further observed a growing tendency amongst academics to somewhat ‘fetishize’ workers’ perspectives
F57.claim: a core researcher's stated limit: the danger of hearing workers only through institutional attention, and academics' tendency to fetishize workers' perspectives

F58.locus: ¶ 'Celebrating the launch of the Data Workers Inquiry Project'
F58.quote: The project is a global and radically participatory research initiative that lets data workers themselves become community researchers. It is led by Weizenbaum Institute researcher and our close collaborator, Dr. Milagros Miceli.
F58.claim: SUPERRR: a global, radically participatory initiative led by Milagros Miceli
F58.lineage: what it is: data workers' own research in their workplaces

F59.quote: the initiative doesn’t reduce data workers to research subjects but empowers them to be community researchers by providing them with fair wages, a methodology, and a platform to conduct their own individual inquiries.
F59.claim: the initiative pays the community researchers fair wages and gives them a method and a platform

F60.quote: working in a job where he and other workers impersonate an AI sex chatbot
F60.claim: an inquiry by a worker who, with others, impersonates an AI sex chatbot
F60.lineage: workers who perform as the machine

F61.locus: SEPTEMBER – Organizing the Data Workers Transnational Assembly in Berlin
F61.quote: Most data workers have to sign Non-Disclosure Agreements that prohibit them from speaking about their projects or the tasks that they completed, making it almost impossible to prove their work experience and expertise
F61.claim: most data workers sign NDAs that bar them from speaking of their tasks, making their expertise hard to prove
F61.lineage: non-disclosure agreements and the risk of speaking

F62.claim: SUPERRR and the project organized the Data Worker Transnational Assembly in Berlin (September 2025)

F65.quote: PRESS RELEASE: The Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) and Weizenbaum Institute launch the Data Worker’s Inquiry repository and talk series.
F65.claim: DAIR and the Weizenbaum Institute launch the repository and a talk series
F65.date: 2024-07 (launch event 8 July, the year from B5)

F66.quote: The Data Workers’ Inquiry is a community-based research project in which data workers from all over the world conduct individual inquiries. From reports and animations to powerful documentaries and zines, the Data Workers‘ Inquiry repository presents a multifaceted view of the realities confronted by data workers, ranging from psychological, physical, and sexual abuse, to resistance strategies and efforts to unionize.
F66.claim: the press release's definition, and the repository's range, from psychological, physical and sexual abuse to resistance and unionizing
F66.date: 2024-07 (launch event 8 July, the year from B5)

F67.quote: The data workers who are tasked with the labor-intensive and emotionally taxing work of data labeling, content moderation, and other forms of data processing that enable AI systems to function, are often located in the Global Majority, precariously employed, and politically dispersed. The Data Workers’ Inquiry provides a platform for them to conduct their own research and describe issues in their own words.
F67.claim: data workers doing labeling, moderation and other processing that enables AI are often in the Global Majority, precarious and politically dispersed; the project gives them a platform for their own research
F67.lineage: whose labor: data work that enables AI systems

F68.quote: This community-based research project has brought together 15 data workers from Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon, and Germany, and diverse employment contexts, including various outsourcing companies and platforms. The data workers develop unique research questions, design and conduct their inquiries, and prepare a presentation format for their findings.
F68.claim: 15 data workers from Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon and Germany at launch; they set the questions, conduct the inquiries and choose the format
F68.lineage: scale: the inquirers and their countries

F69.quote: We center their experiences and recognize their unique knowledge. We are proactive supporters, but the epistemic authority remains with the workers.
F69.claim: Miceli: the team supports; epistemic authority remains with the workers

F70.quote: The project repository is a valuable resource for researchers, journalists, and policymakers seeking first-hand accounts of data work … The findings are an urgent call to confront labor inequities and exploitative practices.
F70.claim: the repository serves researchers, journalists and policymakers; Dinika: the findings call for confronting labor inequities

case.statement: The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The Labor Vector census record describes the Data Workers' Inquiry from its own pages and its institutes', each field with its basis ('operator'), and answers for it the census's question of who supplies the labor, who directs it and who receives its gains; the capture record checks the composition against those pages (CAP-1-01). No deposit names the project, its method or its operators' work on it. The deposits bear on its class, the data work whose labor the inquiries record and the hidden labor behind AI, and add senses and limits on the field's own object: data work as semantic labor, invisible, uncompensated and unattributed (#222, #247, #258, #18, #308), as bearing without articulation (#478, #533), as extraction (#623), as ground-truth labor against variance-generative labor (#163), the literature of hidden labor as stopping short of the provenance of meaning (#144), and annotators as not, as such, the Semantic Proletariat (#1545). #163 states its relation to the critical AI-labor literature in these terms: it names AI's labor architecture and does not address the labor type the deposit adds. The census's own reading on task-origin (LV-20) takes the inquiries' documentation as given. No defining paper contests the field's ontology of the project or supplies one the field lacks: ρ = extends, the equal-terms case (§0.9, §1.2a).

loci.quote: This literature names *AI's labor architecture*. What it does not address is the specific labor type relevant to the present argument. Ghost work is *ground-truth labor*: the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true.

E_F.definition: the community-based, radically participatory research project of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) and the Weizenbaum Institute, with TU Berlin (lead Milagros Miceli; Weizenbaum phase August 2023 to November 2024; launched online 8 July 2024), in which data workers, labelers, annotators and content moderators at outsourcing firms and platforms, often in the Global Majority, research their own workplaces with their colleagues as community researchers, setting the questions and choosing the format (zine, documentary, comic, essay, podcast, animation, report), with epistemic authority remaining with them, trained and paid by the organizing team; a renewal of Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry as participatory action research and as the method it names WIRM; its inquiries documenting trauma, refugees' precarity, platform shutdowns, gift-card pay, rejections, personal-data extraction, NDAs, the work of performing as the machine, and organizing; its stated limit that the organizing it accompanied stayed largely local; no Wikipedia article

E_A.definition: the same project, in the Labor Vector census record and the archive's deposits: a participatory research initiative whose evidence is worker testimony and an organizing resource, in the intersections labor producing AI, worker power and AI governing labor; its labor supplied by data workers, directed by outsourcers and platforms for client firms, its gains unrecorded; not a representative survey, not research about workers by outsiders, not a union; answering the workers' own account of their workplaces and not prevalence or wages at scale; read on task-origin where a person performs as the machine; the class whose labor it records read as semantic labor, invisible, uncompensated and unattributed (#222, #247, #258, #18, #308), as bearing without articulation (#478, #533), as extraction (#623), as ground-truth labor (#163), the hidden-labor literature as naming the worker and not the provenance of meaning (#144), and annotators as not, as such, the Semantic Proletariat (#1545); whose composition at its own name held its method and authority and dropped its negative (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29)
